question.prompt: Which of the following is equal to \(\sqrt{9-6\sqrt{2}}+\sqrt{9+6\sqrt{2}}?\)

solutions.explanation:
The radicands have the form \(9-u\) and \(9+u\), so their product will simplify by the difference-of-squares identity. This suggests squaring the whole sum.

Both radicands are positive: \(9>6\sqrt2\) because these are positive numbers and \(81>72\). Let
\[
S=\sqrt{9-6\sqrt2}+\sqrt{9+6\sqrt2}>0.
\]
Using the square-of-a-sum formula and multiplying the nonnegative square roots gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
S^2
&=18+2\sqrt{(9-6\sqrt2)(9+6\sqrt2)}\\
&=18+2\sqrt{81-72}\\
&=18+6=24.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(S>0\), we take the positive square root:
\[
S=\sqrt{24}=2\sqrt6.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{2\sqrt6}\), choice B.
solutions.title: Square the whole sum

solutions.explanation:
To simplify each outer square root, look for a square of the form \((\sqrt a\pm\sqrt b)^2\). The numbers \(6\) and \(3\) work because they add to \(9\) and their radical cross term is \(2\sqrt{18}=6\sqrt2\). Thus
\[
(\sqrt6\pm\sqrt3)^2=9\pm6\sqrt2.
\]
The principal square root of a square is its absolute value. Since \(\sqrt6>\sqrt3\), both \(\sqrt6-\sqrt3\) and \(\sqrt6+\sqrt3\) are positive. Therefore
\[
\sqrt{9-6\sqrt2}=\sqrt6-\sqrt3,
\]
\[
\sqrt{9+6\sqrt2}=\sqrt6+\sqrt3.
\]
Adding cancels the \(\sqrt3\) terms and leaves \(2\sqrt6\). The answer is \(\boxed{2\sqrt6}\), choice B.
